enc.title: Band electrons in a field: wave packets, effective mass, holes

blocks.html: A Bloch state is spread over the whole crystal, so it cannot describe transport. Build a wave packet from Bloch waves within $\Delta k$ of $\mathbf k$: it is localised to $1/\Delta k$. It must be smaller than the mean free path and contain many wave vectors of the zone, $1/l\ll\Delta k\ll1/a$, which only works when $l\gg a$. Expanding $\varepsilon(\mathbf k^\prime)$ around $\mathbf k$ shows that the packet moves with the group velocity (script eqs. 4.10–4.11).

blocks.label: group velocity of a band electron

blocks.html: Newton’s law for quasi-momentum (4.12–4.14): the field does work $dW=-e\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf v\,dt$, and this raises the band energy, $d\varepsilon=\nabla_{\mathbf k}\varepsilon\cdot\dot{\mathbf k}\,dt=\hbar\mathbf v\cdot\dot{\mathbf k}\,dt$. Hence:

blocks.tex: \hbar\dot{\mathbf k}=-e\mathbf E,\qquad \dot v_\alpha=-\frac{e}{\hbar^2}\sum_\beta\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon}{\partial k_\alpha\partial k_\beta}E_\beta,\qquad m^*_{\alpha\beta}=\hbar^2\Big[\frac{\partial^2\varepsilon}{\partial k_\alpha\partial k_\beta}\Big]^{-1}
blocks.label: script eqs. (4.14), (4.15), (4.17)

blocks.html: The effective mass depends on $\mathbf k$. In a cosine band it is positive near the bottom, infinite at the inflection point and negative near the zone boundary. Under a constant force $k$ grows linearly; the electron first speeds up, stops at the zone boundary (zero group velocity), runs backwards, and so on: without scattering it only oscillates (Bloch oscillation) and carries no net current.

All electrons together (script 4.2.3): in a field the whole occupied part of the band creeps through $k$ space. A completely filled band carries no current: for every $\mathbf k$ there is $-\mathbf k$ with the opposite velocity, and a creeping filled band stays filled. A partly filled band would only slosh back and forth. Scattering makes a steady current possible: once there are empty states at lower energy on the back side of the Fermi sea, electrons scatter back, and the creep stops at a steady offset.

Holes: an almost filled band is simpler to describe by its missing electrons. Near the top of a band the electron effective mass is negative; the missing electrons behave as particles with positive charge and positive mass. This explains positive Hall coefficients in some metals and the hole conduction in semiconductors.

Typical question: given $\varepsilon(k)$, compute $v(k)$ and $m^*(k)$, say where $m^*$ diverges or changes sign, and what happens to an electron in a constant field. Sheet 7 Q3 is exactly this with next-nearest-neighbour hopping.

check.q: Where does the effective mass in the band $\varepsilon=E_0-2t\cos ka$ diverge?
Why does a completely filled band carry no current?
options: Its electrons at $\mathbf k$ and $-\mathbf k$ have opposite velocities, and a field only moves electrons within the filled band
check.explain: Script 4.2.3: the creeping filled band remains filled, so the velocities still cancel.

check.q: Without any scattering, a constant electric field makes a band electron
check.explain: $k$ runs through the zone again and again, the velocity changes sign every half period.

enc.title: Effective mass and Bloch oscillations in a cosine band
enc.goal: An electron in the band $\varepsilon(k)=E_0-2t\cos ka$ ($t>0$) is in a constant field $E$ along $x$. Find (a) $v(k)$, (b) $m^*(k)$ and where it diverges or is negative, (c) $k(t)$ and $x(t)$ without scattering: amplitude and period. (d) Why is this never seen in a metal?

steps.reveal: $v(k)=\frac{2ta}\hbar\sin ka$: zero at the band bottom and at the zone boundary, largest at $ka=\pm\pi/2$.

$\frac{d^2\varepsilon}{dk^2}=2ta^2\cos ka$, so $m^*=\frac{\hbar^2}{2ta^2\cos ka}$: positive for $|ka|<\pi/2$, infinite at $|ka|=\pi/2$, negative beyond. At the bottom, $m^*=\hbar^2/(2ta^2)$: a narrow band (small $t$) means heavy electrons.

$k(t)=k_0-\frac{eE}\hbar t$. $x(t)=\int v\,dt=\frac{2t}{eE}\cos\big(k(t)a\big)+\text{const}$ (check: $\dot x=\frac{2t}{eE}\cdot a\sin(ka)\frac{eE}\hbar=v$). The electron oscillates over a distance $4t/(eE)$ (peak to peak) with the period $T_B=\frac{2\pi\hbar}{eEa}$, the time to cross the zone $2\pi/a$.

For $a=3$ Å and $E=10^5$ V/m: $T_B=\frac{2\pi\hbar}{eEa}\approx1.4\times10^{-10}$ s, while electrons scatter every $\tau\sim10^{-14}$ s. They never complete a fraction of an oscillation; scattering turns the creep into a steady current (script 4.2.3). Bloch oscillations are seen only in superlattices with a large period $a$.

enc.title: Carrier statistics: intrinsic and doped semiconductors

blocks.html: Electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band, per volume (script 5.2.1): count the states times their occupation.

Two approximations make this easy: parabolic bands near the edges with masses $m_e^*$, $m_h^*$, so $\nu(\varepsilon)=\frac1{2\pi^2}\big(\frac{2m_e^*}{\hbar^2}\big)^{3/2}\sqrt{\varepsilon-\varepsilon_c}$ (spin included), and Boltzmann tails, because $\varepsilon_c-\epsilon_F$ and $\epsilon_F-\varepsilon_v$ are many $k_BT$: $f\approx e^{-(\varepsilon-\epsilon_F)/k_BT}$ and $1-f\approx e^{-(\epsilon_F-\varepsilon)/k_BT}$. With $x=(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_c)/k_BT$ and $\int_0^\infty\sqrt xe^{-x}dx=\frac{\sqrt\pi}2$:

blocks.label: script eqs. (5.9)–(5.13); effective density of states
mass-action law (5.15), intrinsic density (5.16), chemical potential (5.14)

blocks.html: The product $n_en_h$ does not depend on $\epsilon_F$: doping raises one density and lowers the other. In an intrinsic semiconductor the chemical potential sits in the middle of the gap, shifted towards the lighter band. Order of magnitude: $n^{\text{eff}}\approx2.5\times10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$ for $m^*=m_e$ at 300 K.
Doped (script 5.3.2, donors $N_d$ with ionisation energy $E_d$ below the conduction band): electrons on the donors follow the Fermi function, and the conduction electrons come from ionised donors.

Three regimes as the temperature rises: donor ionisation ($k_BT\ll E_d$): $n\approx\sqrt{N_dn_e^{\text{eff}}}e^{-E_d/2k_BT}$ (5.27); exhaustion ($E_d\ll k_BT\ll\Delta$): all donors ionised, $n\approx N_d$, flat; intrinsic: carriers across the gap win, $n\propto e^{-\Delta/2k_BT}$. The chemical potential moves from just below the conduction band, below the donor level, down to mid-gap.

The script uses $E_d$ in two ways: in (5.24)–(5.26), $\varepsilon_c-E_d$ is written for the donor level, so $E_d$ is the ionisation energy; in one sentence of 5.3.2 the "donor ionization energy" is called $\varepsilon_c-E_d$. Read $E_d$ as the ionisation energy, as the formulas require.

An Arrhenius plot $\ln n$ against $1/T$ has slope $-E_d/2k_B$ in the ionisation regime and $-\Delta/2k_B$ in the intrinsic regime, with a plateau at $N_d$ in between. Old exams ask for the gap or the donor energy from such a plot.

check.q: Doping raises $n_e$ by a factor 100. What happens to $n_h$?
check.explain: Mass action: $n_en_h$ is fixed at given $T$ (eq. 5.15).

check.q: In the exhaustion regime of an n-type semiconductor the electron density is
check.explain: All donors are ionised, the valence band does not yet contribute (script 5.3.2).

check.q: An Arrhenius plot of the intrinsic regime gives the slope
check.explain: $n\propto e^{-\Delta/2k_BT}$: the factor 2 comes from the square root of the mass-action law.

enc.title: Intrinsic carrier density and where the chemical potential sits
enc.goal: Parabolic conduction and valence bands with masses $m_e^*$, $m_h^*$ and gap $\Delta=\varepsilon_c-\varepsilon_v\gg k_BT$. Derive $n_e$ and $n_h$, the chemical potential of the neutral (intrinsic) crystal and the intrinsic density. Evaluate $n^{\text{eff}}$ for $m^*=m_e$ at 300 K.

steps.reveal: $f\approx e^{-(\varepsilon-\epsilon_F)/k_BT}$; with $x=(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_c)/k_BT$: $n_e=\frac1{2\pi^2}\big(\frac{2m_e^*k_BT}{\hbar^2}\big)^{3/2}e^{(\epsilon_F-\varepsilon_c)/k_BT}\frac{\sqrt\pi}2=2\big(\frac{m_e^*k_BT}{2\pi\hbar^2}\big)^{3/2}e^{(\epsilon_F-\varepsilon_c)/k_BT}$.
Likewise with $1-f\approx e^{-(\epsilon_F-\varepsilon)/k_BT}$: $n_h=n_h^{\text{eff}}e^{(\varepsilon_v-\epsilon_F)/k_BT}$.
$n_e=n_h$: $e^{(2\epsilon_F-\varepsilon_c-\varepsilon_v)/k_BT}=(m_h^*/m_e^*)^{3/2}$, so $\epsilon_F=\frac{\varepsilon_c+\varepsilon_v}2+\frac34k_BT\ln\frac{m_h^*}{m_e^*}$ (eq. 5.14).

steps.prompt: Mass action and the intrinsic density.
steps.reveal: $n_en_h=n_e^{\text{eff}}n_h^{\text{eff}}e^{-\Delta/k_BT}$, independent of $\epsilon_F$; neutral: $n_i=\sqrt{n_e^{\text{eff}}n_h^{\text{eff}}}\,e^{-\Delta/2k_BT}$.

$\frac{m_ek_BT}{2\pi\hbar^2}=5.4\times10^{16}$ m$^{-2}$ at 300 K, so $n^{\text{eff}}=2.5\times10^{25}$ m$^{-3}=2.5\times10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$. For Si ($\Delta=1.12$ eV, $k_BT=25.9$ meV): $e^{-\Delta/2k_BT}\approx4\times10^{-10}$, so $n_i\sim10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$, against $\sim10^{23}$ cm$^{-3}$ atoms.

keyPoints: Boltzmann tails and the $\sqrt x\,e^{-x}$ integral

enc.title: The diode equation
enc.goal: A p–n junction with built-in voltage $V$ and an applied bias $U$ (forward: $+$ on the p side). Derive the current–voltage characteristic from the generation and recombination currents.
given: The bias drops across the depletion layer: the barrier becomes $V^\prime=V-U$ (eq. 5.47)

steps.reveal: Minority carriers created thermally near the depletion layer (electrons on the p side, holes on the n side) are swept across by its field, whatever the barrier: $j_e^{\text{gen}}$, $j_h^{\text{gen}}$ do not depend on $U$ (both negative in the script’s sign convention).
Majority carriers must climb the barrier $e(V-U)$ to cross and recombine on the other side: $j^{\text{rec}}\propto e^{-e(V-U)/k_BT}$, exponentially sensitive to $U$.
Without bias nothing flows: $j_h^{\text{rec}}(0)+j_h^{\text{gen}}=0$ and the same for electrons (eqs. 5.49, 5.50). Hence $j^{\text{rec}}(U)=-j^{\text{gen}}e^{eU/k_BT}$.
$j=|j_h^{\text{gen}}+j_e^{\text{gen}}|\big(e^{eU/k_BT}-1\big)$: exponential growth in forward bias, a small saturated current $-|j^{\text{gen}}|$ in reverse bias. A rectifier.

blocks.html: One spin ½ in a field $\mathbf H=H\hat z$ (script 6.2.1): moments $\mu_\sigma=\frac{g\mu_B}2\sigma$, Zeeman energies $\varepsilon_\sigma=-\mu_\sigma\mu_0H$, Boltzmann occupation.

blocks.label: Curie law for spin $S$, eq. (6.11); for $S=\frac12$, $S(S+1)/3=\frac14$

blocks.html: Metals do not follow Curie: their spin susceptibility is small and temperature-independent. Pauli (script 6.2.2): almost all states are filled with an up and a down electron, which cannot flip. A field shifts the two spin bands by $\mp\frac{g\mu_B\mu_0H}{2}$ at a common Fermi energy; the extra up electrons and missing down electrons sit in a sliver at $\epsilon_F$.

The hand-waving version gives the same: only about $\nu(\epsilon_F)k_BT$ electrons can respond, each with a Curie susceptibility $\propto1/k_BT$; the temperatures cancel (eq. 6.12). Compared with free spins, $\chi_P/\chi_{\text{Curie}}\sim k_BT/\epsilon_F\sim10^{-2}$ at room temperature. Landau diamagnetism of the orbital motion is $-\frac13\chi_P$ for free electrons (script 6.2.3).

check.q: Why is the spin susceptibility of a metal temperature-independent?
options: Only electrons within $\sim k_BT$ of $\epsilon_F$ can flip, and each responds like $1/k_BT$
The spins are locked by exchange
check.explain: The number of active electrons grows like $T$, each one’s response falls like $1/T$ (script eq. 6.12).

enc.title: Curie law for spin ½
enc.goal: $N$ independent spins ½ in a volume $V$ ($V_0=V/N$), field $H$ along $z$. Derive $\langle\mu\rangle(H,T)$ and the low-field susceptibility $\chi$.

steps.reveal: $p_\sigma=\frac{e^{-\varepsilon_\sigma/k_BT}}{\sum_{\sigma^\prime}e^{-\varepsilon_{\sigma^\prime}/k_BT}}$ with $\varepsilon_\pm=\mp\frac{g\mu_B\mu_0H}2$.
$\langle\mu\rangle=\frac{g\mu_B}2(p_+-p_-)=\frac{g\mu_B}2\tanh\frac{g\mu_B\mu_0H}{2k_BT}$.
$\tanh y\approx y$: $\langle\mu\rangle=\frac{(g\mu_B)^2}{4k_BT}\mu_0H$; saturation $\frac{g\mu_B}2$ for $g\mu_B\mu_0H\gg k_BT$.
$M=\langle\mu\rangle/V_0$, so $\chi=\frac{\partial M}{\partial H}=\frac{\mu_0(g\mu_B)^2}{4k_BTV_0}=\frac CT$: the Curie law.

enc.title: Pauli susceptibility from shifted spin bands
enc.goal: A free-electron metal with density of states $\nu(\varepsilon)$ (both spins together) in a field $H$, $k_BT\ll\epsilon_F$. Derive the magnetisation and $\chi_P$.

steps.reveal: At a common Fermi energy, $\frac{N_\sigma}V=\int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon_F}\frac{\nu(\varepsilon-\sigma g\mu_B\mu_0H/2)}2d\varepsilon=\int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon_F+\sigma g\mu_B\mu_0H/2}\frac{\nu(\varepsilon)}2d\varepsilon$ (eq. 6.14).
$\frac{N_+-N_-}V=\int_{\epsilon_F-g\mu_B\mu_0H/2}^{\epsilon_F+g\mu_B\mu_0H/2}\frac{\nu}2d\varepsilon\approx\frac{\nu(\epsilon_F)}2g\mu_B\mu_0H$.

$M_z= rac{g\mu_B}2 rac{N_+-N_-}V=\mu_0 rac{(g\mu_B)^2}4H
u(\epsilon_F)$, so $\chi_P=\mu_0 rac{(g\mu_B)^2}4

enc.title: Exchange and mean-field magnets in depth

blocks.html: Where exchange comes from (script 6.3.1): two ions, one unpaired electron each, orbitals $\psi_1$, $\psi_2$. The two-electron state must be antisymmetric: a symmetric orbital part $\psi_S=\psi_1(\mathbf r_1)\psi_2(\mathbf r_2)+\psi_2(\mathbf r_1)\psi_1(\mathbf r_2)$ goes with the spin singlet, the antisymmetric $\psi_T$ with the triplet. The Coulomb repulsion gives the two different energies $E_S$ and $E_T$. Within these four states the Coulomb Hamiltonian acts exactly like a spin Hamiltonian:

blocks.tex: \hat H_{\text{spin}}=\frac{E_S+3E_T}4-(E_S-E_T)\,\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2\ \ \Rightarrow\ \ \hat H_{\text{Heisenberg}}=-J\,\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2,\quad J=E_S-E_T
blocks.label: script eqs. (6.44), (6.45); check with $\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2=\frac14$ (triplet), $-\frac34$ (singlet), $\hbar=1$

blocks.html: For the crystal, $\mathcal H=\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}-J_{ij}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j$ (6.47): $J>0$ ferromagnetic, $J<0$ antiferromagnetic in the script’s convention. Mean field (6.50–6.56): replace the neighbours by their average, $\mathbf S_j\to\langle\mathbf S\rangle$; every spin feels the Weiss field $\mathbf H_{\text{inter}}=\frac{J_{\text{total}}V_0}{(g\mu_B)^2\mu_0}\mathbf M$ with $J_{\text{total}}=JZ$.

Ferromagnet below $T_C$ (6.3.4): the magnetisation must produce the Weiss field that produces it: $M=M_S\big(\frac{|J|Z}{(g\mu_B)^2\mu_0}V_0M,T\big)$ (6.68). Solve graphically: $y=x$ against the single-spin curve. If the slope of the curve at the origin, $\frac{|J|ZV_0}{(g\mu_B)^2\mu_0}\frac CT$, exceeds 1, a nonzero solution appears:

blocks.label: script eqs. (6.70)–(6.72); equal to $T_W$ only in mean field

blocks.html: Antiferromagnet (6.3.5): on a bipartite lattice (black and white sublattices) all bonds can be satisfied by the Néel state; the order parameter is the staggered magnetisation $\mathbf L=\mathbf M_1-\mathbf M_2$ (6.73). Each sublattice feels the field of the other, which leads to the same self-consistency for $L$ and the Néel temperature:

On a lattice that is not bipartite (triangular) not all antiferromagnetic bonds can be satisfied: geometric frustration, with unusual spin structures or no order at all. In real materials $T_N$ and $|T_W|$ can differ a lot; a large $|T_W|/T_N$ is a sign of frustration or low dimensionality.

Sign conventions differ between sources: the script writes $\mathcal H=-\sum J\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j$ (ferro for $J>0$), while the HS23 exams of the old course write $+J$ (antiferro for $J>0$). Every exam states its convention: check it before you plug in.

check.explain: $\hat H=-J\hat{\mathbf S}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf S}_2$ is lowest for the triplet when $J>0$ (script 6.45).

enc.title: Mean-field Curie temperature and the magnetisation near it (spin ½)
enc.goal: A Heisenberg ferromagnet with spin ½, $Z$ nearest neighbours and exchange $J>0$, in zero external field. Derive the self-consistency equation for $m=2V_0M/(g\mu_B)\in[-1,1]$, the Curie temperature, and $m(T)$ just below $T_C$.

steps.reveal: Insert the Weiss field: $\frac{g\mu_B\mu_0H_{\text{inter}}}{2k_BT}=\frac{JZ}{4k_BT}m$, so $m=\tanh\Big(\frac{T_C}Tm\Big)$ with $T_C=\frac{JZ}{4k_B}$.
A nonzero solution exists when the slope of $\tanh$ at the origin, $T_C/T$, exceeds 1: $T<T_C=\frac{JZ}{4k_B}$, which is $|J|Z\frac{S(S+1)}{3k_B}$ for $S=\frac12$ (eq. 6.72).
$\tanh y\approx y-\frac{y^3}3$ with $t=T_C/T$: $m=tm-\frac{t^3m^3}3$, so $m^2=\frac{3(t-1)}{t^3}\approx3\big(1-\frac T{T_C}\big)$: $m\approx\sqrt{3(1-T/T_C)}$, the mean-field exponent $\frac12$.
$T\to0$: $m\to1$, full saturation $M=g\mu_B/(2V_0)$. Above $T_C$ only $m=0$; in a field the Curie–Weiss law $\chi=C/(T-T_C)$ follows from linearising.
